p:
Thank you, Chair. Good to see you, Commissioner and to your team. Several streets within the gateway aware of my district within the 42nd council district remains under ownership and jurisdiction of HPD. Now, I’m frustrated as well, because I’ve been in office for close to three and a half years, or two and a half years, and we’ve been getting the same thing, the same response from DOT that the transition’s going to take place, and we’re still waiting. We’re still waiting. So, when are we going to finally get

something done? And I believe this even dates back going five, six, seven, eight, 10 years to my predecessor. We need some solid answers as to when you're going transfer the streets over to DOT, because currently– you know, the streets, there’s no alternate side parking. There’s sanitation concerns. There’s abandonment of cars back there. Our office is constantly getting calls and complaints to deal with those situations. We need DOT– we need you to act. We need DOT, HPD start talking if you're not talking. Figure it out. But we need something done. We can’t– I can’t leave this meeting today and get the same response we got the last time we spoke. We need some type of action.
I hear you loud and clear, Council Member. Give an update.
Yeah, so the good news is that something is actually happening right now because the Department of Design and Construction–
[interposing] What’s the something? What’s the something?
What’s the big [inaudible]
What’s the something? You said something is happening now. [inaudible] Thank you.
Right, something good is happening, yep, in that they’re fixing the streets to comply with DOT standards. So, as you probably know, the streets were built in a way–
[interposing] We did see those, correct.

that we were not going to be able to accept those streets into our ownership unless they were kind of brought up to the proper standards. They’re being fixed by DDC. We're talking about it a lot internally. If you like, we can get on a call and understand when that work will be done and exactly the steps for us to then take the streets into our ownership. But we’ve been working closely to make sure that they’re built in a way that we need them to be built. And so I think it’s finally moving in the right direction.
So, is there more work to be done?
I believe the work is happening–
[interposing] Because I believe it has been completed, because–
[interposing] Okay. I’d have to double-check if it’s been fully–
[interposing] Yeah, because of the portion of the work was actually in front of my office.
Okay.

And it was badly needed. And also, when it comes to the actual– the signs. I see a lot of no standing signs that are placed throughout the entire– that particular area. Residents are getting ticketed and construction is done back there.
Okay.
And that’s another concern, another issue, because you know, those are signs that shouldn’t be there, you know. Folks should be able to–
[interposing] Right, we want to [inaudible]--

park there without those type of barriers that are there now. So, again, we’re looking forward to working with you on this, because the residents– every time I get screamed at, I’m going to scream at you.
Fair enough.
Thank you.
No problem.
Thank you. Deputy Speaker?
Thank you. I know that the Chair asked some of these questions, but does DOT have a map of both red light and speed cameras where they’re, like, located?
We don’t. We don’t have a public map. Although I know that a lot of the driving apps have them.
Okay. So, you have no– you have a map, it’s just not public. But are you able to share that with the Council?
It’s intentionally not shared.
Okay.
because we don’t want to give the impression to the public that–
[interposing] I mean– I know the public, but can you share it with the Council? I know it’s– I know the cameras are not to be shared. Like, I know.
We can certainly follow up with you offline.

I know. Because multiple members of the Council have asked, and I know maybe you can’t put like street corner, but can you at least even share, like, by zip code how many exist if you can’t give location? I don’t understand why this is so difficult.
Yeah. Sorry to sound like we’re benign difficult. Council Member, so as I mentioned earlier, we don’t want people to adjust their behavior–

[interposing] I know, I’m not asking for the map to be shared

publicly. I’m asking if you guys can share it with the Council.
And what– I’ll be honest with you. Even internally we don’t share things, because they–
[interposing] Okay, can you share how many–
[interposing] [inaudible] able to get out.
speed cameras and red light cameras are located by zip code? That’s not– it has nothing to do with–
[interposing] We could definitely do some kind of breakdown.
actual location. You can say– or even by Council District.
Yeah, we can definitely–
[interposing] Council District One has 10 red light cameras and 10 speed cameras.
Yep. Yes. Council Member, definitely we can share type of breakdown like that.
Can you share the breakdown by the end of the day today? Like, we’ve– I know multiple people– I’m like– we’re kind of like up–
[interposing] Yeah.
to our wits end with this.
Understood, yep. I just think that–

[interposing] And largely why I’m asking that question, and I’ll get into like questions right now– is because many members feel like the cameras are disproportionately located in certain communities. We have heard that that is not the case, but because we have no anecdotal– anecdotal– we have no actual data that can actually say that. It’s kind of like hearsay at this point, and so we would love to know where the cameras are across New York City to be able to say whether or not they're equitably distributed across New York City. Okay.
Understood, 100 percent.
Okay.
So, I think like just giving– I don’t know. I’m not sure exactly what time it is, it’s on a Friday. We can aim to try to get you something today, but we’ll probably–
[interposing] I’m just adding pressure, you know.
need a couple work days.
I feel like you guys need deadlines.
Yeah.

Okay. So, one short racial equity goal was actually to review critical finding fee-based programs by 2028 for potential racial and ethnic disparities. So why was this selected as DOT’s only short turn goal? And were other short term goals considered?
so, we–

[interposing] Because this, as you see the theme, right? Like if you have these fee-based programs, red lights, speed cameras, and then you yourself in the racial equity

plan said that you’re going to review these programs, right?
Right. You want to understand. You want some tangible information that supports our statement that they’re not predominantly in one neighborhood–

[interposing] And then in your own racial equity plan that you submitted, you all said that you were going to review the fine and fee based programs. And what do you mean by that? Do you mean just the automated enforcement programs or other things maybe like outdoor dining?

I mean, we don’t have a whole lot of fine and fee-based programs to be honest, and those that we do have a lot of times the fees are stipulated in the legislation or the fees are the same across the board irrespective, you know, of the neighborhood or they may be graduated more based on where there’s more demand, things like outdoor dining. So, yeah. I mean, I was saying, we don’t have a lot of fine and fee based programs. Many of them, those costs are already stipulated. So, there’s not a lot where we’re really– we have

discretionary costs, but I’m not sure if that’s answering your questions.

I mean, we just wanted to know what critical fine and fee-based programs were, because that’s what you all put in the racial equity plan. Okay, I’ll just ask one more question and come back for second round. My understanding is that DOT has previously found no racial or ethnic disparities with respect to its automated enforcement programs as well as many of the DOT programs. Were those previous assessments insufficient or inaccurate? Because I don’t– it doesn’t seem like anybody on this dais has any idea of the racial equity plan that you put forward. So, you all said that you wanted to review the fine and fee-based programs, right, as a means of determining whether or not there are any disparities based off of race and ethnicity in New York City. But previously DOT has said that you didn’t find anything. And so the question is, is that what you might have assessed in the past was inaccurate which is why you are now suggesting that this should be something to review, just want to understand. And again, also based off of like both community and Council Members who have

said repeatedly that they feel like the cameras specifically are located in primarily communities of color.

So, Council Member, for every– every program I think we want to continually be checking year after year that nothing is going astray and we’re not enforcing or providing anything in a way that’s hurting one community over another. So, if there seems like there’s a contradiction there, it’s just that we want to keep checking year after year.
Yeah. My understanding is that the previous assessments did not find disparities, but these programs are always changing and dynamic. So we do assess them on a regular basis, absolutely.
Okay. Round two. If we could actually switch the clock to two minutes, because I know we’re pressed up for time. But for round two we have Council Member one, Won and then Epstein.

Thank you so much. So, to pivot, I want to go back to with One LIC [sic], through this rezoning, the city committed to

creating a new waterfront esplanade and open space under the Queensboro Bridge by 2031, including $79 million in capital funding. On page 303 of the Capital Plan, all that funding has a planned commitment date of 2031, project ID SEEDHWQ7. Can you clarify the start date for the funding for this project, and will this be funding– will this funding present any delays of the city’s complete– commitment to complete the new open space by 2031?

Thank you for the question, Council Member. First of all, I want to say that any movement in the Capital Plan does not signify any delay, and we’re moving steadfast on the commitments made in the rezoning. Given capital structures, we’ve had to move some funding around, but we’re working with EDC and other partners to make sure that it’s moving as quickly as we promised in the points of agreement.
So, is that a yes or a no? Is there any funding delays for the city’s commitment?
There are no funding delays.
There are no funding delays to open this park by 2031?
There are no funding delays.

Okay. So we want to see this open by 2031. As Part of One LIC, the city made the following commitments to street safety and public realm improvement projects. One of them was $1.25 million for a comprehensive lighting study in [inaudible] IBZ to be completed by 2026, $700,000 for an automated public toilet at Court Square to be completed by 2027, $250,000 for a study of possible public realm improvements under the Queensboro Bridge ramps to be completed by 2027. Can you clarify whether the funding is commitment to these projects in the Executive Budget?
We’re fully funded for all the commitments made in the points of agreement in the rezoning, and they’re all moving forward as promised.
Okay. Do you know what page we can find these projects, because we’ve been reading every single page and we could not find it?
I think you might be looking in the Capital Plan, but they’re folded into some of our expense reports.
Okay, thank you.
So, that might be the confusion.

Can I just ask one more question? Okay. On the timeline of these projects funded, so we’re seeing that– you are saying on record that the timelines of the commitment will be on the POA. The city also committed $30 million on pedestrian and cycling infrastructure improvements along the 44th Drive corridor and $13 million to create an intermodal hub at 21st Street Station with designs, both projects beginning in 2089 [sic] to 2029. The capital funds of these projects beginning in 2029 June to June 2032. Can you clarify the start date for the capital funding of the 44th corridor improvements, and will this funding timeline present any delays to the city’s committed timeline to begin design 28, and do you expect any need for additional funding to complete these projects?

Thank you for the question, Council Member. So,

we’re actively scoping the projects which means that we’re getting the package ready to transmit to DDC for them to start design. Let me– so, to your last question about other funding needs, no, we feel that what was promised on the POA will be the accurate funding need. We’re in preliminary scoping for 44th Drive right now, and then the Center Auverne [sic] Boulevard project will follow after that.

Okay. Thank you so much for those answers. We’re going to follow up in writing with all these questions and the details, especially on the waterfront greenway and everything else, and we’ll also follow up for written criteria on how you calculate and evaluate what intersections qualify for daylighting. Thank you so much to both the Chairs.
Council Member Wong?
Thank you, Chairs. Really quick answer, please, one line answer. Does DOT travel around looking for potholes or does it rely entirely on 311 complaints?

We do look for potholes in the course of all of the rest

of our work. They’re called in by multiple operational staff.

Okay. Thank you. Next, I went to junior highschool is Maspeth and that was 1979. One of the projects was design a Grand Street Bridge, because the city had plans of replacing it. Fast-forward, we’re now at 2026. I’m glad to see that in this budget that we have $326.1 million for the reconstruction of the Grand Street Bridge over the Newtown Creek. Question, is this money already here? Because I went to the session a couple of days ago and they said it’s federal funds. And my question is, is the money already in place or are you still waiting for it, and what's the timeline for the construction? Thank you.
Thank you for the question, Council Member. So, the– we are fully funded for the Grand Street Bridge and it is projected to go to construction in 2029, fiscal year 2029.
Okay. Thank you. Thank you, Chairs.
79, that’s when I was born. Okay, Council Member Epstein followed by Deputy Speaker.
I thank you, Chair. Can I– is the capital plan for Broadway fully funded at this point, the redesign of Broadway?
Broadway in Manhattan?
Manhattan, sorry, my borough.
My understanding is that the certain segments of it are funded and moving ahead as capital projects.
Great.
You mean– when you say the full corridor you mean–
Mean the 34th down to Union Square, the redesign.
Yes, that’s fully funded.

That’s fully funded. Is that included– I know you’re going to do two new kiosks in there and those are going to have

public water and publicly available water fountains, too?
Yeah, yeah, that is the plan.
We talked about having a publicly available bathroom in that, is that in the new bathroom plan as you anticipate having a publicly available restroom available?
I’m not sure. I’d have to check and get back to you.

Yeah. It's something– you know, obviously we talked to– the mayor’s talked a lot about. Yeah, especially with Madison Park right there, 23rd/Flat Iron area, we’d really like to see a publicly available bathroom in that location. I hope that DOT can commit to doing that.
Yeah. We understand this administration has been very committed to increasing access to public bathrooms, and so we’ll just have to check on that specific question.

And we’re in active scoping, so this is the perfect time

to have that conversation to make sure that the infrastructure is built for public bathroom.

Yeah, I want– I flagged it for your team. I want to make sure. Since the capital is there, I want to make sure the capital available to do– put that infrastructure in place, including the bathrooms and the water fountains and the bottle filler and all the public amenities that we would need in that part of the city.

And I’ll just– I’ll mention on that topic, because I know it is front of mind for many of us, on the public toilets, I believe– you know, the new program that the mayor announced, that EDC should be announcing a selected vendor very soon. So that program’s going to be getting off the ground.
Great. And that’s like the vendor will determine where in the city, what boroughs, what neighborhoods will have?
No, we’ll be working, DOT in some coordination with Parks, to figure out– to figure that out.
Okay. Thank you. With public input, right?
Well, yeah. I think based on where we’re hearing these kinds of– yeah, these types of needs.
Thank you. Thank you, Chair.
Thank you. Deputy Speaker?
Thank you. Just really quickly, the Streamlined Procedures to Expedite Equitable Development, SPEED, will DOT update travel to mayor responses for newly upzoned neighborhoods like Jamaica or LIC?
Sorry, Council Member, can you just clarify travel to responses?

Yeah. So, the SPEED effort as I understand it is to really look at communities that are being upzoned, travel demand, etcetera, and so what I want to know is will you update any information for newly upzoned neighborhoods? Because this is a new thing going forward for this upcoming fiscal year, but there are neighborhoods that are recently rezoned. So, just want to understand if this SPEED effort would apply to them?
So, the SPEED effort specifically is about new rezonings and new developments.
[inaudible]
But we’re also still committed to what we agreed to of doing a very comprehensive traffic study of Jamaica to make sure that we understand exactly how traffic patterns have changed.

I just want to make sure because we just rezoned and then this effort is new, so just want to make sure. That was the question. Like, are you going to also retroactively look at newly rezoned areas, because we just rezoned it last year.
So, yes, we are studying that area. It’s not part of the new funding, but it’s part of the work that we do on a normal course of business.

Okay. Back to the racial equity plan. So, the desired outcome of one of DOT’s midterm goals was to achieve citywide equity and transportation infrastructure by building and implementing a comprehensive plan to serve 100

percent of underserved communities by 2030. This is a laudable goal, but it does seem very vague and unrealistic, and I just think a lot about my community in my southeast Queens where we have a lot of sidewalks and curbs that contribute to a wide range of things like illegal dumping, flooding, etcetera. So, how can DOT achieve this transportation equity goal in underserved neighborhoods by 2030 if according to another one of its long-term goals, DOT does not expect to build meaningful relationships with those underserved communities until 2036? Essentially, none of the indicators for this outcome relate to any new infrastructure investment that would be needed to achieve a citywide equity and transportation goal for infrastructure. So, we just want to understand like why there’s a lack of indicators that match this critical aspect of the outcome.

Thank you, Council Member. I mean, I do want to underscore that transportation equity is central to what we’re doing. I think agency’s made great strides, but it’s going to be even more of a priority in this administration. We’ve brought on some new senior leadership and we’ve

kind of reorganized some of our offices to really create one group that can think holistically around long-term planning, how we embed equity in everything we’re doing. We take it really seriously. You know, one thing we’ve done as part of the New York City’s Streets Plan, it established for the first time a citywide metric for how we measure transportation equity and how we identify underserved neighborhoods and invest in them, and it’s really translating into all of our programs where we’re prioritizing our investments in those top tier equity priority neighborhoods. So, I want to underscore that. I’m not sure– you know, I might have to get back to you on specifically the metrics in the racial equity plan, and we’re happy to do that.

Yes, I would love for y’all to get back to me, because we’re doing a budget hearing now, and if in your goals you set a goal for 100 of underserved communities by 2030 to have equity in transportation infrastructure, to me all of those things carry a price, and so we want to make sure that as we continue towards adoption, that your agency’s budget reflects the resources that can get you to your goal. And I think based off of what

we’ve received it doesn’t, and that there are indicators that don’t really match what you’ve put forward. So, I hope that as you go towards finalizing your racial equity plan that you make the necessary adjustments to actually achieve your goal versus just writing some things on a piece of paper because it may sound good. Thank you.
Understood. Thank you.

Thank you. I’m going to ask a question on behalf of Council Member Brooks-Powers, but this is actually an issue I know that is very important to myself as well as the Deputy Speaker and a bunch of other Council Members, on the tractor trailer overnight parking. Because on September 28th, 2023, the Council passed a bill that requires the city to create off-street parking for tractor trailers because this has been a huge issue for us, and it requires DOT, DCAS, DCP to coordinate on creating that off-street parking by December 31st, 2025 which has already passed. So, just in the interest of time, where have you identified those commercial parking– off-street commercial parking lots, and also can you provide an update on the

timeline as well as how much it’s going to cost to build municipal lots. So, where, how long and the cost?

So, yes. Thank you for the question. We’ve been very aware of the issues with overnight truck parking and the new federal rules that have really put pressure on that. As you mentioned, we did work– we have been working with a lot of our sister agencies around the requirements of that law. So for example, DOT looked at all the land that we owned which includes, you know, public parking lots now as well as other pieces of land that we own, and we determined that we, DOT, don’t have space that’s appropriate for use in that context, but we are working with our other sister agencies as EDC and others lead that effort. So, we– at the same time, we’ve recognized that this is a big problem and that’s why we’ve been setting up on the street metered overnight truck parking in industrial districts where it belongs. That’s why the Council passed another bill really encouraging us to focus on those areas last year. And so we have been studying IBZs and other appropriate areas around the city for where we can provide more of that overnight truck

parking so that it’s not showing up in places where it’s not appropriate. So, we– while, you know, that particular study is beyond DOT, we are still as an agency very invested in doing a lot of work to provide that overnight truck parking in appropriate places.

How about DCAS, DCP, other agencies private parking lots, I know that have been interested in renting out their spaces. How have those conversations been going? Because we’re past the deadline. So I just wanted to get a sense of when.

Yeah. I think as long as the facilities work functionally. Like, obviously the trucks need a lot of space to be able to maneuver, and so that’s a big part of the conversations. That’s one of the limiting factors, but as Deputy Commissioner Beaton said, those are active conversations. We’re committed to trying to support this goal. I know I also bring it up every time I meet with like the Trucking Association of New York or others, I just really underscore, because we know this is a big issue for communities.
Yeah. If you can follow up with the timeline, that’d be great. And then also my last question is just around if you coordinate with NYPD regarding the illegal truck parking enforcement?
